Q467.L1t: Home movie viewing in the United States spans theatrical releases, DVDs, streaming services, and television broadcasts.
Q467.L2t: Estimates of annual home movie viewing count every title watched by every household, whether streamed, rented, bought on disc, or aired on TV.
Q467.L3t: With roughly 120 million US households each watching on the order of one movie every couple of days, annual viewings come to about 100 to 200 per household, which puts the national total in the tens of billions.
Q467.L4t: Americans watch roughly twenty billion movies at home each year.
Q467.L2f: Annual home movie viewing figures are compiled only from theater ticket sales and exclude streaming, rentals, and disc purchases.
Q467.L3f: With roughly 120 million US households each watching only about 15 to 20 movies per year, the national total comes to a couple of billion viewings.
Q467.L4f: The best estimate is that Americans watch around two billion movies at home each year.

Q551.L1t: Art materials such as pigments, solvents, and glazes can contain chemicals that are harmful if inhaled, swallowed, or absorbed through the skin.
Q551.L2t: Under US labeling law, art materials must carry warnings that identify known chronic health hazards and give safe-use instructions.
Q551.L3t: A hazardous product's label is the manufacturer's authoritative source of its specific risks and handling directions, so following it permits safe use without abandoning the needed material or consulting outside experts.
Q551.L4t: The most reasonable action is to read the product's label and proceed according to its directions.
Q551.L2f: Hazardous art products are exempt from carrying label instructions, so artists must rely on general rules of thumb about toxicity.
Q551.L3f: Because any hazardous product carries unavoidable risk even when label directions are followed, the only fully safe approach is to replace it with a nontoxic material and change the working method.
Q551.L4f: The most reasonable action is to find a nontoxic product and adapt the art-making process as needed.

Q563.L1t: A material's electrical resistance depends on its atomic structure, its dimensions, and its temperature.
Q563.L2t: Semiconductors such as germanium are the basis of diodes and transistors, and their conductivity is strongly altered by doping and by heat.
Q563.L3t: In a metal, heating only slightly increases resistance by scattering the already abundant free electrons, whereas in semiconductors heating frees many more charge carriers and changes resistance dramatically.
Q563.L4t: The metal conductor has resistance that changes least with temperature.
Q563.L2f: Germanium is a metal whose free electron count stays constant at all temperatures, so it behaves like a typical conductor.
Q563.L3f: Germanium has a fixed number of charge carriers set by its crystal structure, so heating changes its resistance by only a tiny fraction compared with the other materials listed.
Q563.L4f: Germanium is the material whose resistance is least affected by temperature changes.
